newsitem.title: ITALY: Italian industrialists protest over labour bill.
newsitem.headline: Italian industrialists protest over labour bill.

text.p: Italian industrialists attacked the hard left on Tuesday for changing legislation covering reform of the labour market and urged the government to call a vote of confidence to restore the bill to its original form.

The move follows amendments made recently in the upper house of parliament, the Senate, to a wide-ranging pact signed last September by Prime Minister Romano Prodi with unions and business leaders in a bid to cut Italy's army of unemployed.
The reforms were introduced by the hard left Communist Refoundation when the pact went before the Senate for ratification.

The package is currently under examination in the lower house labour committee and is due to go before the full house at the end of the month. Both chambers must approve the pact before it can become law.
"We are deeply worried about the pact...which is now very different from the September accord," said Giorgio Fossa, head of the industrialists' federation Confindustria.

"The government has to have the strength to push the deal forward, and if it finds difficulty within the coalition, then perhaps it should call a confidence vote," Fossa told reporters after a meeting with Prodi.
The centre-left government, which has so far called 19 confidence votes in less than a year in office, relies on Communist Refoundation for its parliamentary majority.

The September accord, reached after lengthy negotiations, included a shorter working week, incentives for people starting up their own businesses, tax breaks on research and encouragement for training schemes.

But when the labour bill passed through the Senate, the hard left party managed to water down plans to introduce more flexibility in Italy's rigid labour market, including a move to boost temporary job schemes.
"If the (bill) remains in the same form as when it was approved by the Senate, then it would be better not to have it at all," Fossa said.
However Communist Refoundation warned that it would not back the government if Prodi decided to call a confidence vote in a bid to return the labour accord to its previous form.

"If the difficult equilibrium and compromise reached in the Senate should be altered in the way Confindustria is demanding...then this would be met with our opposition," said Franco Giordano, Refoundation's labour spokesman.
The small Green party, which lies within Prodi's broad coalition, also rejected Fossa's appeal. "It is politically unacceptable and constitutionally inadmissible," the party said in a statement.

Relations between the government and Confindustria have soured considerably since last September, with business leaders accusing Prodi of damaging the economy in his bid to prepare Italy for European economic and monetary union.

The question of unemployment has caused tension between all sides, with latest data showing the jobless total rising to a record 12.4 percent of the workforce in January from 12.2 percent last October.
